questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Ethanenitrile is treated with LiAlH4 in dry ether. The main organic product is:
questions.explanation: LiAlH4 reduces the C≡N group completely to CH2NH2, so CH3CN gives CH3CH2NH2 with the same number of carbon atoms. Methanamine would be the Hofmann bromamide product of ethanamide, which loses one carbon, and ethanal needs a partial reduction of the nitrile by SnCl2/HCl followed by hydrolysis.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry Part II, Ch 13 Amines: preparation of primary amines by reduction of nitriles

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Butan-1-ol and butan-1-amine have almost the same molar mass, yet butan-1-ol boils at a much higher temperature. This is mainly because:

options.text: O–H···O hydrogen bonds are stronger than N–H···N hydrogen bonds
butan-1-amine molecules cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other
butan-1-ol has a longer carbon chain than butan-1-amine
nitrogen is more electronegative than oxygen, so N–H is more polar

questions.explanation: Oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen, so O–H is more polar and the O–H···O hydrogen bonds of the alcohol are stronger than the N–H···N bonds of the amine. Primary amines do form hydrogen bonds, so the amine is not free of them, but both compounds have four carbons and nearly equal masses, so neither chain length nor mass explains the gap.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry Part II, Ch 13 Amines: physical properties: boiling point and hydrogen bonding in amines and alcohols

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem:
Arrange the following in increasing order of reactivity towards electrophilic bromination of the benzene ring:
(A) Aniline
(B) Benzene
(C) Acetanilide
(D) Nitrobenzene
questions.explanation: The lone pair of NH2 is donated strongly into the ring, so aniline is the most reactive. In acetanilide the nitrogen lone pair is also pulled towards the carbonyl group, so activation is weaker than in aniline but still greater than in benzene, while the NO2 group withdraws electrons and deactivates the ring. Placing acetanilide below benzene confuses weaker activation with deactivation.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry Part II, Ch 13 Amines: electrophilic substitution of aniline and the effect of acetylation on ring reactivity

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Aniline is treated with ethanoyl chloride in the presence of pyridine. The role of pyridine is to:

options.text: convert ethanoyl chloride into the less reactive ethanoic anhydride
neutralise the HCl formed and shift the equilibrium towards the product
protonate aniline so that its nitrogen becomes more nucleophilic
prevent the benzene ring from undergoing Friedel-Crafts acylation

questions.explanation: Acylation of the N–H bond releases HCl, which would protonate the amine and push the reversible reaction backwards. A base stronger than the amine, such as pyridine, removes the HCl so that acetanilide forms completely. Protonating aniline would remove its lone pair and make it less, not more, nucleophilic.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry Part II, Ch 13 Amines: chemical reactions: acylation of amines

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: What mass of sodium nitrite (molar mass 69 g mol−1) is needed to diazotise all the aniline used in the preparation?
questions.explanation: Each NH2 group consumes one molecule of nitrous acid, so 0.10 mol of aniline needs 0.10 mol of NaNO2, which is 0.10 × 69 = 6.9 g. Using two moles of nitrite per mole of aniline would give 13.8 g, but only one nitrous acid is used up; the extra hydrochloric acid, not nitrite, is what is taken in excess.
questions.passage_text:
In a laboratory preparation, 9.3 g of aniline (0.10 mol) is dissolved in an excess of dilute hydrochloric acid, and the flask is kept in an ice-salt bath so that the temperature stays between 273 K and 278 K. A cold solution containing exactly the stoichiometric amount of sodium nitrite is added slowly with stirring. The clear solution obtained is never allowed to warm up and is used at once, without isolating any solid from it. It is then divided into four equal portions, labelled P, Q, R and S.

Portion P is poured into a cold alkaline solution of phenol, and an orange-red solid separates at once. Portion Q is treated with aqueous potassium iodide at room temperature; bubbles of a colourless gas escape and a dense, dark oil settles at the bottom. Portion R is added to a warm solution of cuprous cyanide and potassium cyanide; the same colourless gas is evolved, and a colourless liquid with a bitter-almond smell distils over. Portion S is simply left on the bench in a warm room for an hour; it also evolves the colourless gas, and its smell changes to that of a phenolic disinfectant.

Every reaction in this preparation goes to completion, and the organic products from P, Q and R all retain the benzene ring of the original aniline.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry Part II, Ch 13 Amines: diazotisation of aniline: stoichiometry of NaNO2 and HCl

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: The orange-red solid obtained from portion P is:
questions.explanation: Alkaline phenol gives the phenoxide ion, an activated ring that the diazonium cation attacks at the para position in a coupling reaction, producing the orange azo dye 4-hydroxyazobenzene. 4-Aminoazobenzene would need aniline as the coupling partner, and azobenzene and azoxybenzene are reduction products of nitrobenzene.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: The colourless liquid distilled from portion R is boiled with dilute hydrochloric acid until it is completely hydrolysed. The organic product is:
questions.explanation: Cuprous cyanide replaces the diazonium group by CN (Sandmeyer reaction), so portion R gives benzonitrile. Complete acid hydrolysis converts C≡N through the amide into COOH, giving benzoic acid with the same number of carbons. Benzamide is only the intermediate stage, and phenylacetic acid would need benzyl cyanide, which has an extra CH2.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Portion Q releases its gas completely. What volume of the gas, measured at STP, is evolved? (Molar volume at STP = 22.4 L mol−1)
questions.explanation: Each mole of diazonium ion loses one mole of N2. Portion Q holds one quarter of 0.10 mol, which is 0.025 mol, so the volume is 0.025 × 22.4 L = 0.56 L = 560 mL. A volume of 2240 mL comes from forgetting that the solution was split into four equal portions and using the full 0.10 mol.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about the portions P, Q, R and S:
(A) Portion Q forms iodobenzene without needing a copper(I) catalyst.
(B) In portion P the diazonium ion attacks the phenoxide ring as a nucleophile.
(C) The phenolic smell of portion S arises because the diazonium ion is hydrolysed on warming.
(D) In portion R the diazonium group is replaced by CN with the help of a copper(I) salt.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
questions.explanation: Iodide replaces the diazonium group directly without copper, warm water hydrolyses the diazonium ion to phenol with loss of N2, and cuprous cyanide replaces the diazonium group by CN in a Sandmeyer reaction. In coupling the diazonium ion is the electrophile, not a nucleophile, so statement (B) is false; the phenoxide ring is the electron-rich partner.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I: (A) Peptide bond (B) Glycosidic linkage (C) Phosphodiester linkage (D) Disulphide bridge
List-II: (I) Joins two nucleotides (II) Joins two cysteine residues (III) Joins two amino acids (IV) Joins two monosaccharide units
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
questions.explanation: A peptide bond (–CO–NH–) links two amino acids, a glycosidic linkage joins two monosaccharides through oxygen, a phosphodiester linkage joins the sugars of successive nucleotides, and a disulphide bridge forms between two cysteine side chains. Swapping the peptide bond with the disulphide bridge is the commonest slip, because both occur in proteins.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry Part II, Ch 14 Biomolecules: linkages in carbohydrates, proteins and nucleic acids

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem:
Arrange the following in increasing order of molar mass (the same base is present in each):
(A) Nucleotide
(B) Polynucleotide chain
(C) Nitrogenous base
(D) Nucleoside
questions.explanation: A nucleoside is a base plus a sugar and a nucleotide is a nucleoside plus a phosphate group, so the mass rises from base to nucleoside to nucleotide, and a polynucleotide chain, made of many nucleotides, is the heaviest. Putting the nucleotide after the chain would treat it as a polymer, which it is not.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry Part II, Ch 14 Biomolecules: nucleic acids: base, nucleoside, nucleotide and polynucleotide

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about carbohydrates:
(A) Maltose is a reducing sugar because one of its two glucose units has a free hemiacetal –OH group.
(B) Sucrose reduces Tollens’ reagent because it contains a free aldehyde group.
(C) The letter D in D-glucose refers to the configuration at the carbon farthest from the carbonyl group, the same as in D-glyceraldehyde.
(D) Lactose gives D-galactose and D-glucose on hydrolysis.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
questions.explanation: In maltose one glucose unit keeps a free anomeric –OH, so it reduces Tollens’ reagent; D in D-glucose denotes the configuration at C-5 relative to D-glyceraldehyde, not the direction of optical rotation; and lactose is a galactose–glucose disaccharide. Sucrose is non-reducing because both anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond, so statement (B) is false.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry Part II, Ch 14 Biomolecules: disaccharides: maltose, sucrose and lactose; D and L configuration

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: The high specificity of an enzyme for its substrate is best explained by:

options.text: the enzyme shifting the equilibrium of the reaction towards the products
a metal ion that is present in every enzyme molecule
the complementary fit between the active site and the substrate
the high temperature at which enzymes work best

questions.explanation: In the lock-and-key picture only a substrate whose shape and functional groups complement the active site can bind, which is why urease acts on urea but not on similar amides. An enzyme lowers the activation energy but does not shift the position of equilibrium.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry Part II, Ch 14 Biomolecules: enzymes: lock-and-key model and specificity

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Which one of the following hormones is a steroid?
questions.explanation: Testosterone, like the oestrogens and cortisol, is built on the steroid ring system. Insulin is a polypeptide hormone, while thyroxine and norepinephrine are amino acid derivatives formed from tyrosine.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry Part II, Ch 14 Biomolecules: hormones: classification into steroids, polypeptides and amino acid derivatives

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Deficiency of which vitamin leads to pernicious anaemia?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin), obtained from meat, fish, eggs and milk, is needed for red blood cell formation, and its lack causes pernicious anaemia. Lack of vitamin B6 causes convulsions, of vitamin K delayed blood clotting, and of vitamin E increased fragility of red blood cells.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry Part II, Ch 14 Biomolecules: vitamins: sources and deficiency diseases

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: In reverse osmosis used for purifying water, the solvent passes from the solution to the pure solvent through a semipermeable membrane when the pressure applied on the solution is:

options.text: equal to the osmotic pressure of the solution
greater than the osmotic pressure of the solution
less than the osmotic pressure of the solution
equal to the vapour pressure of the pure solvent

questions.explanation: When the applied pressure exceeds the osmotic pressure, the natural flow is reversed and solvent is forced out of the solution, leaving the dissolved salts behind. At equal pressure there is no net flow, and at a lower pressure ordinary osmosis still moves solvent into the solution.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry Part I, Ch 1 Solutions: osmosis, osmotic pressure and reverse osmosis

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Two volatile liquids X and Y form an ideal solution. At a given temperature the vapour pressures of pure X and pure Y are 300 mmHg and 200 mmHg respectively. For a liquid containing equal numbers of moles of X and Y, the mole fraction of X in the vapour in equilibrium with it is:
questions.explanation: By Raoult’s law pX = 0.5 × 300 = 150 mmHg and pY = 0.5 × 200 = 100 mmHg, so the total pressure is 250 mmHg and the mole fraction of X in the vapour is 150/250 = 0.60. The value 0.50 is the liquid composition, which wrongly assumes that the vapour has the same composition as the liquid.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry Part I, Ch 1 Solutions: Raoult’s law for liquid-liquid solutions and composition of the vapour phase

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: A non-volatile, non-electrolyte solute weighing 1.5 g is dissolved in 50 g of cyclohexane, and the freezing point falls by 3.0 K. Kf for cyclohexane is 20 K kg mol−1. The molar mass of the solute is:
questions.explanation: M2 = Kf × w2 × 1000 / (ΔTf × w1) = 20 × 1.5 × 1000 / (3.0 × 50) = 200 g mol−1. Check: molality = 3.0/20 = 0.15 mol kg−1, so moles in 0.050 kg = 0.0075 and 1.5 g / 0.0075 mol = 200 g mol−1. Using 100 g as the solvent mass would wrongly give 100 g mol−1.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry Part I, Ch 1 Solutions: depression of freezing point and determination of molar mass

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: A solute AB2 dissociates in water as AB2 → A2+ + 2B−. A 0.10 molal aqueous solution of AB2 is 50% dissociated. Kb for water is 0.50 K kg mol−1. The elevation in boiling point of the solution is:
questions.explanation: The Van’t Hoff factor is i = 1 + α(n − 1) = 1 + 0.5 × 2 = 2, so ΔTb = i Kb m = 2 × 0.50 × 0.10 = 0.10 K. Check by counting particles: 0.05 AB2 + 0.05 A2+ + 0.10 B− = 0.20 mol per kg. Taking complete dissociation (i = 3) gives 0.15 K, and ignoring dissociation (i = 1) gives 0.050 K.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry Part I, Ch 1 Solutions: Van’t Hoff factor, degree of dissociation and elevation of boiling point

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about azeotropes:
(A) The composition of an azeotropic mixture changes continuously during its distillation.
(B) A solution showing positive deviation from Raoult’s law can form a minimum-boiling azeotrope.
(C) An azeotropic mixture cannot be separated into its components by fractional distillation.
(D) A mixture of nitric acid and water containing about 68% nitric acid is a maximum-boiling azeotrope.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
questions.explanation: Azeotropes boil at constant temperature with vapour and liquid of the same composition, so they cannot be separated by fractional distillation. Positive deviation gives a minimum-boiling azeotrope, and nitric acid with water (about 68% acid) is the textbook maximum-boiling case from negative deviation. The first statement describes an ordinary mixture, not an azeotrope.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry Part I, Ch 1 Solutions: non-ideal solutions and azeotropes (elementary idea)
